Data_Protection_Law: Canada regulates federal public bodies under the Privacy Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. P-21) and private-sector organizations under the Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act (PIPEDA) (S.C. 2000, c. 5). Three provinces have “substantially similar” private-sector laws—Québec’s Act respecting the protection of personal information in the private sector (modernized by 2021, c. 25 (“Law 25”)), Alberta’s Personal Information Protection Act, and British Columbia’s Personal Information Protection Act—which generally apply to provincially regulated activities in place of PIPEDA; PIPEDA still governs cross-border and federally regulated activities.
DPA_Independence: The Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada is an independent Agent of Parliament that oversees compliance with the Privacy Act and PIPEDA and reports directly to Parliament rather than to a minister.
Children_Data_Safeguards: Under PIPEDA, organizations must obtain “meaningful consent,” and OPC guidance stresses heightened protections for children; consent practices must match a child’s maturity and, for young children who cannot meaningfully consent, be obtained from a parent/guardian. Québec’s Law 25 further strengthens safeguards for minors, including privacy-by-default and a requirement that the holder of parental authority consent to the collection of personal information about a child under 14, subject to the child’s best interests.
COP_Strategy: Canada maintains a National Strategy for the Protection of Children from Sexual Exploitation on the Internet led by Public Safety Canada, supporting the RCMP’s National Child Exploitation Crime Centre and the Canadian Centre for Child Protection.
SOGI_Sensitive_Data: OPC interpretation treats information about sexual orientation and an individual’s sex life as generally “sensitive,” typically requiring stronger safeguards and a higher threshold for collection and use under PIPEDA.
LGBTQ_Legal_Status: Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since the Civil Marriage Act (S.C. 2005, c. 33). The Canadian Human Rights Act prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation and, since 2017 (Bill C-16), expressly includes gender identity or expression. The Criminal Code’s hate-propaganda framework applies to “identifiable groups,” including sexual orientation and gender identity/expression.
Promotion_Propaganda_Offences: Canada does not criminalize the “promotion” of LGBTQ identities; instead, the Criminal Code prohibits advocating genocide (s.318) and the public incitement or wilful promotion of hatred against an identifiable group (s.319). “Conversion therapy” is expressly criminalized by 2021, c. 24 (in force Jan. 7, 2022).
AI_Policy_Status: There is no stand-alone federal AI statute in force; federal departments are bound by the Treasury Board’s Directive on Automated Decision-Making (2019), which requires Algorithmic Impact Assessments, tiered safeguards, transparency and human oversight. The Pan-Canadian Artificial Intelligence Strategy (2017; renewed 2022) is a national funding program supporting AI research and talent (not a regulatory law).
DPIA_Required_High_Risk_AI: Federal institutions must conduct Privacy Impact Assessments for programs/activities that involve personal information under the Treasury Board Directive; Québec’s Law 25 requires privacy impact assessments for projects involving systems or services that process personal information, capturing many higher-risk automated/AI deployments in that province.
SIM_Biometric_ID_Linkage: No federal statute mandates SIM registration linked to a national ID or to biometrics. Wireless services are governed by the Telecommunications Act and the CRTC’s Wireless Code; carriers may verify identity for service/credit purposes, but there is no requirement to register SIMs with biometric data, and any biometric collection would be subject to PIPEDA’s consent and necessity limits.
